demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson is about the kit's own rows, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: Label the frozen rows yourself, blind
demos.purpose: Do it: your sheet Open evals/reports/judge_labels.csv in a spreadsheet or a text editor. For each row, read the context first, then the answer, then the question again, and write yes or no under both label columns. Write a note on any row you hesitate over, now: step 4 prints it beside the other reader's. Here is one filled row of the kit's fixture, as a sheet holds it: The answer refuses, so it claims nothing: grounded, yes. But the context holds the cap, so a refusal does not answer the question: no. The reader's note says why: "the cap is in the context". Save the sheet as CSV with every column kept and in the same order. A spreadsheet may add a byte-order mark, Windows line endings or a capitalised YES; the check reads all three. Then check it:

demos.heading: Kappa by hand, and the judge's own reasons
demos.purpose: Two standard-library cells over the files themselves, with no kit function between you and the count. The first cell reads your sheet and the author's with Python's csv module, counts p_o and p_e by hand, and checks the result against the kit's cohen_kappa(). It is this lesson's arithmetic in a screenful, and it runs anywhere Python does. The first cell reads your sheet and the author's with Python's csv module, counts p_o and p_e by hand, and checks the result against the kit's cohen_kappa(). It is this lesson's arithmetic in a screenful, and it runs anywhere Python does. The second reads the judge's ratings file directly and prints each row where the judge and you disagree, with the judge's score and its own explanation. It is lesson 4.2's advice made concrete: where they disagree, read the row. It skips judge_agree.py's row_sha check, because both files come from the same frozen set.
